B: Hello, can you hear me?
A: Hi, yeah, I can hear you. Can you hear me okay? Sorry, my internet's been a bit funny today.
B: Yes, you're fine. I'm Alison.
A: I'm Sana. Nice to meet you.
B: And you. Whereabouts are you, Sana?
A: Luton. Erm, Bury Park, if you know it? Probably not, lol, sorry. It's near the town centre, kind of.
B: I don't, no. I'm in Stockton-on-Tees, in the North East.
A: Oh, that's far. Is it cold up there?
B: It can be. It was quite fresh this morning on my walk. I go along the river most days, down by the Barrage.
A: Oh that's nice. I walk a lot as well, round Wardown Park mostly, or just to my mum's. She's only ten minutes away, so I'm round there, like, every day. She rang me three times this morning just asking if I'm coming for dinner.
B: Three times.
A: Three times! And I'd already said yes the first time.
B: My mam was a bit like that. She'd ring to check you'd got home, and then ring again to check you'd heard her ring.
A: Yeah, that's exactly her. So, erm, what do you do? Sorry, are you working?
B: I'm retired now. I was a medical secretary at a GP practice for twenty-seven years.
A: Oh wow, twenty-seven years. That's so long. You kind of remind me of the manager at my old nursery, actually. That's a good thing, I mean, sorry. She was really organised and everyone sort of relied on her.
B: That's very kind. I think I was the one who knew where everything was filed. You worked in a nursery?
A: Yeah, I was a nursery practitioner, but it closed down about five months ago, so I'm looking for jobs at the minute. Nursery, school, care assistant, whatever's near home really. It's been kind of stressful, not gonna lie. I'm on the job sites every day.
B: That must be hard, when it's not your doing.
A: Yeah. And I still think about the kids, you know, whether they settled in their new places. There was one little boy especially. Anyway, sorry, I'm going on.
B: No, not at all. It sounds like you cared about them. That's not a bad thing in a nursery, is it?
A: No, I suppose not. Do you have grandkids?
B: One. A grandson in Leeds. He's just starting to talk, so every time I see him there's a new word. Last time it was "bus", and he said it about two hundred times.
A: Aww. That age is the best. They just repeat everything. We had one at the nursery who'd only say "no" for a whole month, like, to everything. Do you want your snack? No. Do you want to go outside? No.
B: That sounds like my son at that age. He's thirty-one now and not much has changed.
A: Lol. Do you see your grandson a lot?
B: I drive down every few weeks. Not as often as I'd like, but they're busy.
A: Yeah. I'd love kids soon, but it's, erm, money and everything, you know? We're only in a two-bed.
B: There's never a perfect time, I don't think. I had mine in a small house and we managed.
A: That's what my mum says. She wants grandkids yesterday.
B: Mothers usually do. What do you do with yourself, when you're not job-hunting?
A: I do mehndi, like henna, for weddings. I've got one next month, for my cousin's friend. And I watch way too many dramas with my mum.
